claims.text: Conventional TiB2-reinforced boride-coated steel components have a coarse, heterogeneous microstructure.
Conventional TiB2-reinforced boride-coated steel components exhibit microsegregation and prominent grain boundaries.
Controlled laser surface remelting refines the microstructure of TiB2-reinforced boride coatings.
Laser surface remelting can produce a dense, nanocrystalline boride layer with fewer defects.
Laser remelting induces rapid melting and recrystallization.
Rapid melting and recrystallization eliminate microsegregation.
Laser remelting reduces defects in the boride layer.
A nanocrystalline boride layer has uniformly narrow grain boundaries and reduced defect density.
The refined boride layer acts as a barrier against aluminum diffusion.
The refined microstructure limits diffusion channels available to molten aluminum.
Limiting interfacial diffusion and grain-boundary attack reduces the molten-aluminum corrosion rate.
Laser-treated coatings will have a statistically significantly lower corrosion rate than untreated coatings during otherwise identical molten-aluminum exposure.
Laser-treated coatings will exhibit lower weight loss than untreated coatings during molten-aluminum exposure.
Laser-treated coatings will retain better microstructural integrity than untreated coatings during molten-aluminum exposure.
The corrosion-resistance benefit will remain effective when laser parameters avoid excessive melting and compositional changes.
Treatment efficacy depends on coating thickness and substrate thermal properties.
Different component geometries require separate optimization of the laser treatment.
